title: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Zechariah son of Jehoiada
paragraphs: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Zechariah son of Jehoiada
He died in the church courtyard.

Not in a battlefield.
Not in a pagan temple.
In the place that was supposed to honor God.

Zechariah son of Jehoiada is one of those Bible characters we almost walk past. But once you see him, you cannot unsee him. His story is only a few verses long in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22, yet it lands like thunder. He stood up when a nation bent down. He spoke when a king turned corrupt. He told the truth when truth had a price.
And the price was his blood.

This is the tragedy. King Joash was rescued as a child because of Zechariah’s father, Jehoiada the priest. Jehoiada protected him. Preserved him. Helped place him on the throne. But after Jehoiada died, Joash drifted. Fast. He abandoned the house of the Lord. He listened to flatterers instead of God. Then came Zechariah—filled with the Spirit of God—saying, “Why do you transgress the commandments of the Lord, so that you cannot prosper?” (2 Chronicles 24:20).

That was not political commentary.
That was prophetic mercy.

But here’s what we miss: people often hate the voice that exposes the sin they want to keep. So Joash ordered Zechariah to be stoned. The son of the man who saved the king was murdered by the king he had every reason to trust. Final words burning in the air: “May the Lord see and avenge!” (2 Chronicles 24:22).
What a wound.

Loyalty repaid with betrayal.
Truth repaid with violence.
A righteous man silenced in the courts of God.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Because Zechariah’s story does not only show us a forgotten martyr. It shows us a shadow of Someone greater. Jesus also stood in covenant truth before a rebellious people. Jesus also was rejected, not for sin, but for righteousness. Jesus also was killed by those who should have recognized Him. In fact, when Jesus spoke of the murder of the righteous in Matthew 23:35, He referenced “Zechariah son of Barachiah.” Some scholars interpret that as this Zechariah in 2 Chronicles, while others see a textual or identification complexity there. But the point still burns: God does not forget the blood of His faithful witnesses.
Yet Jesus goes even further.

Zechariah cried, “May the Lord see and avenge.”
Jesus cried, “Father, forgive them.”
That is the Gospel.

We are not only Joash in this story—forgetful, compromised, disloyal. We are the people who resist conviction when it gets too close. We silence truth in quieter ways. We excuse. We delay. We dress rebellion in religious language. But Christ meets traitors with mercy. He takes the judgment our sin deserves, rises in victory, and offers forgiveness to the very ones who nailed truth to the ground.
So no, Zechariah son of Jehoiada is not a minor character.

He is a warning.
He is a witness.
He is a mirror.

Do not overlook the man who spoke truth in the temple and paid for it with his life. And do not overlook the Savior to whom his story points—the One who was slain and yet lives, the One who turns rebels into sons, the One who still calls compromised hearts back home.

Repent while your heart is still tender.
Return while grace is still reaching.
Run to Jesus while the door is still open.
